title: What do five numbers look like in the Mesopotamian system?
description: Five numbers are grouped by the landmarks one, sixty and three thousand six hundred, and then written by their counts in the places. Two of the numbers have a place with no count, which is left blank.
teaching_notes: One idea: group by landmarks, write the counts in their places, and leave a blank where a landmark does not occur. Watch for students who squeeze the numbers together and skip the blank place.

video_script.why: The child uses the grouping by landmarks of four thousand and the dropping of symbols from the place value example to write five numbers, two of them with a blank place.
video_script.substitution: The numbers are smaller, and in two of them a landmark does not occur, so its place is left blank.
video_script.anchor: the book's Mesopotamian places: ones on the right, sixties next, then three thousand six hundreds
video_script.payoff_line: Sixty is one and a blank, and three thousand six hundred five is one, a blank, and five.

final_answer.spoken: sixty three is one, three; one hundred thirty two is two, twelve; two hundred is three, twenty; sixty is one and a blank; three thousand six hundred five is one, a blank, and five

maths_rules: landmarks 1, 60, 3600; counts below 60 in each place
(iv) 60 = (1) x 60, the 1s place is empty, written 1 followed by a blank
(v) 3605 = (1) x 3600 + 5, no 60s, so the 60s place is empty, written 1 | blank | 5
video_script.design: One idea: a landmark that does not occur leaves a blank place. The places stay on the board and a blank is drawn as an empty box.

beats.on_screen: small title card From your book; the numbers 63, 132, 200, 60 and 3605 in a column, each with an empty row of places beside it

marks.book: the title card From your book appears
marks.nums: the five numbers appear in a column

narration: <bookmark mark='book'/>This is a question from your book about the Mesopotamian system.
<bookmark mark='nums'/>We must write sixty three, one hundred thirty two, two hundred, sixty, and three thousand six hundred five.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>How will each number look in its places?

beats.on_screen: the question stays on the board with the empty places

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: three places labelled 3600, 60 and 1 from the left; a count drops into each place; a place with no count stays as an empty box

marks.group: a number is grouped by the landmarks 1, 60 and 3600
marks.drop: the counts drop into the places
marks.blank: a place with no count stays as an empty box

narration: <bookmark mark='group'/>As in your book, we group each number by the landmarks. They are one, sixty and three thousand six hundred.
<bookmark mark='drop'/>Then we write only the counts, each in the place of its landmark.
<bookmark mark='blank'/>A place with no count is left blank.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, five numbers, sixty three, one hundred thirty two, two hundred, sixty, and three thousand six hundred five.

beats.on_screen: To find: each number in the Mesopotamian places

marks.find: the words each number in the places are written

narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to write each of them in the Mesopotamian places.

marks.sixty3: 63 = (1) x 60 + 3 is written and the counts 1 and 3 drop into the places
marks.onethirty: two 60s = 120 and 132 - 120 = 12 are written and the counts 2 and 12 drop into the places

narration: <bookmark mark='sixty3'/>Step one, take sixty three first. It has one sixty and three left over, so it is written one, then three.
<bookmark mark='onethirty'/>Next, one hundred thirty two has two sixties, which make one hundred twenty. Twelve is left, so it is written two, then twelve.

beats.on_screen: (iii) 200: three 60s = 180, 200 - 180 = 20, written 3 | 20. (iv) 60 = (1) x 60, the 1s place is empty

marks.two00: three 60s = 180 and 200 - 180 = 20 are written and the counts 3 and 20 drop into the places
marks.sixty: 60 = (1) x 60 is written and the 1s place stays as an empty box

narration: <bookmark mark='two00'/>Step two, take two hundred. Three sixties make one hundred eighty, and twenty is left, so it is written three, then twenty.
<bookmark mark='sixty'/>Sixty is exactly one sixty with nothing left. The ones place has no count, so it is written one, then a blank.

beats.on_screen: (v) 3605 = (1) x 3600 + 5; no 60 fits in 5, so the 60s place is empty

marks.big: 3605 = (1) x 3600 + 5 is written and the counts 1 and 5 drop into the outer places
marks.gap: the 60s place stays as an empty box between them

narration: <bookmark mark='big'/>Step three, take three thousand six hundred five. One three thousand six hundred fits, and five is left.
<bookmark mark='gap'/>No sixty fits in five, so the sixties place has no count. It stays empty between the other two.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Step four, check each one by value. One sixty and three make sixty three, and two sixties and twelve make one hundred thirty two.
<bookmark mark='check2'/>Three sixties and twenty make two hundred. One sixty and no ones make sixty.
<bookmark mark='check3'/>One three thousand six hundred, no sixties and five ones make three thousand six hundred five.

marks.ans: the first three answers are boxed
marks.blank: the last two answers are boxed with their blank places shown

narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Sixty three is one, three. One hundred thirty two is two, twelve. Two hundred is three, twenty.
<bookmark mark='blank'/>Sixty is one and a blank, and three thousand six hundred five is one, a blank, and five.
